text: This video shows that in doeff, a library for algebraic effects in Python, a handler decides how a paused function goes on. A doeff handler receives k, the rest of that function. We compare it with an asyncio task.
When an asyncio task pauses, the loop has two moves: send the result once the future is done, or throw CancelledError into it.
A doeff handler receives k, the rest of the paused function. What happens next is the handler's decision.
Resume k with a value, and the function goes on from its yield.
Throw into k, and the function sees the exception at its yield, where its own except clause can catch it.
Keep k for later, and you have concurrency. scheduled holds the k of each task and goes back to it when the task can go on.
Or never resume k. The run ends with the handler's own value, and the paused generators are closed, so their finally blocks run.
Neither model goes on twice. k is one-shot, like a coroutine object.
But greet() gives a program, not a paused run. Each run starts a new generator, so one program runs under ada, then under grace.
